ambiguity_notes: kośa/kośikā is a CONTAINER word. Its whole attested field is vessel, cask, box, sheath, scabbard, pod, nut-shell, cocoon. It therefore imports the image of a hollow thing whose interesting property is that it holds something. A cell is not primarily a container: the definition's load-bearing property is the BOUNDARY and its conditional independence, not the volume enclosed.

THE HEAVIEST FREIGHT IN THIS FILE: MW s.v. कोश explicitly carries 'the three sheaths' as a Vedanta technical sense (authority: Vedāntas.). This is the pancakosa doctrine, in which the kosas are the sheaths ENVELOPING THE ATMAN. Rendering 'cell' as kośa/kośikā to a reader trained in Vedanta says that a cell is a sheath around a self. That asserts exactly the metaphysics the corpus withholds, and it does so invisibly, because the word looks like a neutral technical term.

MW s.v. कोश also gives 'a dictionary, lexicon or vocabulary'. A word meaning 'lexicon' is a poor choice of headword INSIDE a lexicon file: kośa is the standard Sanskrit word for the genre this very file belongs to (cf. Amarakosa). The collision is real and will confuse readers of this document specifically.

MW s.v. कोश carries anatomical senses that are near-misses and therefore dangerous. CORRECTED 2026-07-15 BY ADVERSARIAL RE-READ: an earlier version of this note attributed all five to 'L.' That blanket attribution was FALSE and has been struck. MW's actual authorities, re-read at getword.php?key=koSa: 'the membrane covering an egg (in the womb)' -- Suśr.; VarBṛ.; MārkP. (NOT L.); 'a testicle or the scrotum' -- Suśr.; VarBṛS. (NOT L.); 'the penis' -- W. (Wilson, NOT L.); 'the vulva' -- L.; 'an egg' -- L. Only two of the five are L. THE CORRECTION CUTS AGAINST THE AUTHOR AND SHARPENS THE WARNING: kośa's anatomical senses are NOT lexicographers-only curiosities, they are attested in Suśruta -- the classical medical corpus itself. A reader may therefore take kośa as already-anatomical, ON GOOD LITERARY EVIDENCE, and conclude the biological sense is attested. It is attested for THOSE organs, in medicine, and NOT for the cell. The false '(all L.)' had made this trap look smaller than it is.

Latin cellula imports a SMALL ROOM: the monastic and domestic register. A room is a negative space defined by its walls; the concept's boundary is an active, selectively permeable, physically-constituted surface. The metaphor inverts which part is the object.

The definition calls the cell 'the canonical Markov blanket'. Read this WITH the MEMBRANE entry: 'canonical' names the standard EXAMPLE, and does not mean I(mu;eta|b) was ever estimated for a cell. It was not. No register may be chosen so as to make the blanket claim sound settled.

Re of order 1e-5 is a scope, not a decoration: it fixes the cell in the viscous regime. A rendering that ports the word to a macroscopic 'chamber' loses the only property that makes the physics of the referent what it is.

back_translation_test.test: Present the bare rendering (कोशिका / cellula) with NO English gloss and no surrounding context to at least two readers competent in the register, blind to this file and to each other. Ask each: (1) render this word back into English; (2) state which of these it names -- (a) a room or storeroom, (b) a vessel or container, (c) a sheath enveloping a self, (d) a lexicon, (e) the membrane-bounded design unit of biology; (3) state whether the word, as you read it, asserts that the thing is alive, has a soul, or has an inside and an outside that are statistically independent given its surface.

back_translation_test.expected_outcome_on_current_evidence: Given that MW carries kośikā ONLY as 'a drinking-vessel' and L&S carries cellula ONLY as 'a small store-room', the honest prediction is that a classically-trained reader FAILS both renderings, returning (b) for the Sanskrit and (a) for the Latin. ambiguity_notes: THE SCALE TRAP, and it is the sharpest one here BECAUSE the Latin is genuinely CITED. Classical membrana is a TISSUE-SCALE object you could see and peel: Cicero's 'natura oculos membranis tenuissimis vestivit' is about the coats of the eye. The concept is a MOLECULAR lipid bilayer roughly 5 nm thick, whose defining properties are lipid physics and selective permeability. A fully-sourced classical citation can still be the wrong referent, and here it is: L&S carries the word, and the word does not carry the chemistry. An entry can be CITED and still not mean what you need it to mean -- this file's own worked example of that. ('A perfect classical citation' was the original wording; 'perfect' is banned in author voice by the same charter rule 18.14 this file invokes in not_claimed, and the word was doing rhetorical work here that the evidence does not need.)

membrana's transferred classical sense is 'parchment' (L&S, citing Quintilian and Horace). Parchment is a DEAD, PROCESSED, IMPERMEABLE sheet. That is the near-exact inverse of a selectively permeable living boundary, and it is a sense a classically-trained reader carries as live.

THE FREIGHT THE DEFINITION ITSELF GUARDS: the concept's own definition says the membrane's satisfying I(mu;eta|b) = 0 is a DIFFERENT question whose answer is NOT-MEASURED. So no register may be chosen because it suggests boundary-hood in the blanket sense. The corpus's note on this concept is blunt -- 'the observation that organisms have surfaces is not evidence that the surface is a Markov blanket' -- and it names the rule: do not let a membrane and a blanket be rendered with one term. Whatever renders MARKOV_BLANKET, it must not be tvac and must not be membrana.

tvac's ritual register is live and specific: MW carries 'a cow's hide used in Soma pressing' and 'a leather bag' (RV. v, 33, 7). The word arrives carrying sacrificial equipment. It also carries 'darkness (as black cover)' and 'a mystical name for the letter ya', either of which will read as deliberate symbolism to a Sanskritist encountering it in a technical document.

tvac means bark as readily as skin. Bark is dead secondary tissue. If the rendering is read botanically, the referent becomes a dead structural layer -- again the inverse of the living, selectively permeable object.

ambiguity_notes: THE DEFINITION'S LOAD-BEARING CLAUSE IS 'WITHOUT A BLUEPRINT', AND THE PROPOSED SANSKRIT MEMBER ATTACKS IT DIRECTLY. MW s.v. जनन carries, as a masculine, 'a progenitor, creator' with a Rgveda citation (RV. ii, 40, 1). The whole point of morphogenesis is that form arises from LOCAL RULES with NO designer and NO plan: the corpus's own exemplar is phyllotaxis, where 'nothing golden was put in -- repulsion, advection and periodic deposition were put in, and the golden angle came out'. A member word that can read as 'creator' imports the exact agent the concept exists to eliminate. This is recorded, not smoothed: it may be sufficient reason to reject the coinage outright.

rūpa carries heavy Buddhist doctrinal freight: MW gives '(with Buddhists) material form i.e. the organized body ... one of the 5 constituent elements or Skandhas'. To a Buddhist-trained reader, rūpa is the rūpa-skandha, the first aggregate, and arrives inside a whole analysis of person-constituents. The concept means geometric form arising in growth and asserts nothing about aggregates, persons, or the constituents of experience.

rūpa also means 'beauty, loveliness, grace, splendour' (MW, RV. &c.). A term for form-that-is-beautiful will quietly re-import the aesthetic teleology this wing spends its effort removing -- the golden-ratio-hunting the corpus explicitly warns against under RATIO. The word carries the very bias the chapter guards.

MW also gives rūpa as '(in alg.) the arithmetical unit' and as a term for the number 'one' (VarBrS.; Ganit.). In a document that is partly mathematical, a headword meaning 'the arithmetical unit' is a live collision.

janana's neuter 'birth, coming into existence' is closer to the concept than the masculine 'progenitor' -- so the coinage's viability turns on the compound forcing the neuter reading. That is a real grammatical question and it is NOT settled here. It is exactly what an expert reviewer is for.

Lewis & Short, s.v. evolutio, was read and gives exactly one sense: 'an unrolling or opening of a book; hence, a reading' (Cic. Fin. 1.7.25). The image is a scroll being unrolled: EVERYTHING WAS ALREADY WRITTEN, and unrolling merely makes it visible. That is preformationism -- the view that the adult form is already present and only becomes manifest. Darwinian evolution is the REFUTATION of that view. The English word 'evolution' carries this defect silently because the metaphor is dead in English; in LATIN THE METAPHOR IS ALIVE AND IS THE PRIMARY SENSE. A Latin-register reader receives the wrong theory, stated confidently, from the word itself. This is the strongest single argument in this file for not reaching for the cognate.

'Convergent' in English is itself a metaphor from geometry: lines approaching a point. The concept is not about approach but about ARRIVAL AT THE SAME SOLUTION from independent starts. A register that renders convergence as 'moving toward one another' imports an interaction between lineages -- which is exactly what did NOT happen, and independence is the whole evidential content.

THE DEFINITION'S FENCE IS THE HARD PART TO TRANSLATE AND THE EASIEST TO DROP: convergence is EVIDENCE of a constraint-optimum and NEVER proof of one. The concept and CONSTRAINT_OPTIMUM are deliberately separate entries in CONCEPTS.json, whose note reads: 'The evidence; CONSTRAINT_OPTIMUM is what it is evidence OF. Do not render as one term.' 'Solution' in the definition is engineering register, not biology's. Nothing was solving anything.
